Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | The Histopathological Types | 1. Minimal lesion GN | (Minimal Change Disease — MCD) | LM: | Normal or mild increase in mesangial cells | EM: | Fusion of foot processes of epithelial cells (podocytes) | IF: | No deposits | 2. Membranous GN (MGN) | LM: | Diffuse thickening of glomerular basement membrane. | 3. Proliferative GN | • Diffuse proliferative: | proliferation of all glomerular cells (endothelial, epithelial & mesangial) | a) Acute diffuse proliferative GN | b) Diffuse proliferation with crescents (Crescentic GN, RPGN) | c) Mesangio-proliferative (MPGN): increased mesangial cells & matrix | d) Mesangio-capillary GN (MCGN): proliferation of mesangial cells & matrix + thickening of glomerular BM | • Focal proliferative: | a) Focal segmental GN (FSGN): cellular proliferation of some segments in some glomeruli | 4. Focal segmental glomerulo-sclerosis (FSGS) | Sclerosis of some segments in some glomeruli. | Contrast: | FSGS = | sclerosis | (scarring) vs FSGN = | cellular proliferation | of segments. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 3

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Clinical Presentations — The 5 Major Syndromes | Acute GN (acute nephritic syndrome) | Onset: | Relatively abrupt | Features: | Hematuria, Proteinuria, Oliguria, Edema, Hypertension | Pathology: | DPGN | Course: | Spontaneous resolution | Nephrotic syndrome | Onset: | Variable | Features: | Albumin < 2.5 g/dl, Proteinuria ≥ 3+, Hyperlipidemia, Edema, Hypertension (MCGN) | Pathology: | Variable lesions | Course: | Variable | Notes: | Variable onset, pathology & course | Chronic GN | Onset: | Insidious / progressive | Features: | Proteinuria 0/1+, Hypertension, Urinary sediments +, Slow progressive decline in GFR | Pathology: | Glomerulosclerosis, chronic interstitial fibrosis | Course: | Progress to renal failure | Notes: | The common pathway to ESRD | Rapidly Progressive GN (RPGN) | Onset: | Rapid decline in GFR | Features: | Hematuria, Proteinuria, Oliguria, Absent or mild hypertension | Pathology: | DPGN with crescents | Course: | Rapidly progresses to AKI | Notes: | Renal emergency — intensive therapy | Asymptomatic proteinuria ± hematuria | Onset: | Insidious | Features: | Hematuria / proteinuria, Hypertension +/–, Normal GFR | Pathology: | FSGN | Course: | Persists or recurs | Notes: | Accidentally discovered, relatively benign | Key: | Every glomerulopathy presents as one (or more) of these 5 clinical syndromes: acute GN, nephrotic syndrome, chronic GN, RPGN, or asymptomatic proteinuria ± hematuria. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 3–4

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Investigations — I (Urine, Blood, Imaging, Biopsy) | 1. Urine Examination | Volume in 24 hours: may be decreased or normal | 24-hour urinary protein or urinary protein/creatinine ratio | Microscopic examination of urinary sediment: | – Red cells → may or may not be present | – | Dysmorphic red cells | → strongly suggestive of GN | – Casts → granular & | red cell casts | (diagnostic of acute GN) | 2. Blood Examination | Blood urea | Serum creatinine | Serum electrolytes (Ca, PO4, K+, Na+) | Assessment of GFR (normal = 90–120 ml/min) | 3. Renal Imaging | Ultrasound | (to exclude other renal pathology): | – Smooth renal outline | – Normal pelvicalyceal system and lower urinary tract | 4. Renal Biopsy — needed for: | Accurate histopathological diagnosis | Assess severity & response to treatment | Prognosis | Note: | Renal biopsy gives the | histopathological diagnosis | , assesses | severity & response to treatment | , and predicts | prognosis | . | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 4–5

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Investigations — II: Specific Investigations (determination of the cause) | Disease / cause | Specific investigation | Diabetes mellitus | Blood glucose | Recent streptococcal infection | ASOT and throat or skin swab | Systemic disease, e.g. SLE | ANA & anti-ds DNA | Goodpasture's disease | Anti-GBM antibody | IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease) | Serum IgA antibody | Low complement states | Serum complement is decreased in: | a) | Post-infection | — acute post-streptococcal GN (transient, 8 weeks), infective endocarditis, and shunt nephropathy | b) | SLE | c) | Cryoglobulinemia | d) | Serum sickness | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 4–5

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Principles of Treatment — I: General Measures | Aims of general treatment | Control of symptoms | Prevent complications | Slow progression of the disease | Diet | Salt & water restriction | for edematous and/or hypertensive patients, especially with oliguria. | Protein intake — remember: | – High protein intake → increases proteinuria in renal failure patients and causes nephron damage → | progression of renal disease | . | – Low protein intake → negative nitrogen balance and malnutrition. | Therefore: | • Normal GFR → physiological needs (1 mg/kg/day) + daily urinary protein loss | • ↓ GFR → moderate protein restriction (0.6–0.8 gm/kg/day) to control anorexia, nausea, vomiting | Control of Edema | Bed rest | Salt restriction (< 2 gm/day) & fluid restriction | Diuretics — preferably | loop diuretics | ; thiazides can be combined | Salt-poor albumin (in resistant cases with hypoalbuminemia) | Ultrafiltration | Hemodialysis | Control of Proteinuria | 1. Avoid high-protein diet (0.8–1 gm/day + estimated daily loss) | 2. Use of | ACEIs & ARBs | : | Both compete with the vasoconstrictor (VC) effect of angiotensin II on the | efferent arterioles | → efferent arteriole vasodilation → decrease intraglomerular pressure → decrease GFR → decrease glomerular filtered protein → | decrease proteinuria | . | NB: | ACEIs are used in small doses in normotensive patients, and used cautiously in renal failure and in hyperkalemic patients. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 5

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Principles of Treatment — II: Hypertension, Lipids, Thrombosis | Control of Hypertension | Value of BP control: | Relief of symptoms | Prevent hypertensive complications on other systems | Decrease progression of renal disease (renoprotective) | Target BP — according to degree of proteinuria: | If proteinuria | > 1 gm/day | → target BP | < 125/75 | (mean BP < 92) | If proteinuria | < 1 gm/day | → target BP | < 130/80 | (mean BP < 98) | Choice of antihypertensive agent: | ACEIs / ARBs | Calcium-channel blockers (CCB) | All have | renoprotective effect | Control of Hyperlipidemia | Avoid high-fat diet | Physical activity | Use statins | Control of Hypercoagulability & Thrombosis | Prophylactic anticoagulation | should be employed in nephrotic syndrome patients at high risk of thromboembolism: | • Increased risk of | venous thrombosis | (albumin < 2.5) → | anticoagulants | • Increased risk of | arterial thrombosis | → | aspirin | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 5–6

Ch 01 · Principles of Glomerulopathies | Specific Treatment & Course | In Primary GN | Immunosuppressive + Cytotoxic drugs | Other measures, e.g. | plasma exchange | In Secondary GN | Treatment of the cause, e.g.: control of infection, treat malignancy, stop toxins & drugs, control of disease activity (SLE, DM, Gout). | Course — variable depending on renal pathology & etiology | Anti-GBM & ANCA-associated crescentic GN | → rapid progression to | ESRD unless treated | . | IgA nephropathy & FSGS | → indolent but persistent course → renal failure. | Post-streptococcal GN | → tends to | resolve completely | with little risk of progression to ESRD. | MGN | → unpredictable: may remit spontaneously, persist / relapse, or progress over years to ESRD. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 6

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Definition | Definition | Acute GN is a clinical syndrome characterized by | acute onset | of: | 1. Hematuria | Macroscopic or microscopic | 2. Proteinuria | < 3.5 gm/d/1.73 m² body surface area | 3. Hypertension | 4. Edema | 5. Oliguria | < 300 ml/day in severe cases | Nephritic vs Nephrotic | Proteinuria is | non-nephrotic range | (< 3.5 gm/day) in acute GN. | Contrast: | The | nephritic syndrome | (acute GN) is dominated by | hematuria | , whereas the | nephrotic syndrome | is dominated by heavy proteinuria ≥ 3.5 gm/day. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 7

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Clinical Features — A. Manifestations of Acute Nephritis | Hematuria | 1. Hematuria | — due to damage of the glomerular capillary walls. It may be: | Macroscopic hematuria | Color of urine depends on pH: | • | Red | urine → in alkaline urine | • | Smoky (or reddish brown) | urine → in acidic urine, due to denaturation of hemoglobin with formation of | acid haematine | and prolonged transit time through the nephron | • Formation of | methemoglobin | gives the smoky color of urine | Microscopic hematuria | Characterized by the presence of | dysmorphic red cells | : | • Small & distorted — due to | mechanical injury | of RBCs passing through the damaged glomerular capillary walls | • Have low hemoglobin content | • Best seen by | phase contrast microscopy | Proteinuria | 2. Proteinuria | — glomerular origin (consists mainly of albumin); non-nephrotic range (< 3.5 gm/day). | Due to: | • Increase of glomerular capillary permeability | • Mechanical disruption of glomerular capillary walls | • Altered glomerular hemodynamics | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 7–8

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Clinical Features — Edema, Hypertension, Oliguria & Associated Disease | 3. Edema | • | Early | → eyelids (puffiness) — as this area is of | low tissue pressure | • Then progresses to involve the legs and other parts | Due to salt and water retention because of: | – Increase reabsorption of filtered Na | + | at the distal tubules | – Decrease GFR → decrease salt delivery to tubules | 4. Hypertension | Due to salt & water retention | , i.e. | volume-dependent | hypertension. | 5. Oliguria | Urine output | < 300 ml/day | . | Due to decreased GFR. | B. Manifestations of the Associated Specific Disease | Manifestations of the associated specific disease, e.g.: | • | Infection | (PSGN) | • | SLE | • | Vasculitis | • | Malignancy | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 8

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Investigations | 1. Urine Examination | Color → red or smoky (dark brown) | Oliguria: < 300 ml/day in severe cases | Proteinuria < 3.5 gm/day | Microscopic examination: | – Hematuria | – | Dysmorphic red cells & red cell casts | — both are pathognomonic for acute GN | – Granular casts | Blood & Imaging | 2. Blood: | (Urea, Creatinine & GFR) — variable impairment of renal function. | 3. Renal imaging: | usually unnecessary. | 4. Renal Biopsy | Most of the renal pathology associated with acute GN is | proliferative | , either focal or diffuse. | Indications for renal biopsy: | A. Unusual clinical features | B. Uncertain diagnosis | C. Rapid deterioration of renal function → | crescentic GN | 5. Specific Investigations | Needed for etiological diagnosis, e.g.: | • | ANA, ds DNA | → SLE | • | Throat swab & ASOT | and | transient decrease of C3 (< 8 weeks) | → PSGN | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 8–9

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Treatment — 1. General Measures | General treatment | To control symptoms and prevent complications. | Home treatment | Hospital admission | For uncomplicated cases | For complicated cases: severe hypertension, renal failure & oliguria, pulmonary edema, encephalopathy | Daily follow-up of blood pressure | Until hematuria, HTN & edema disappear, and proteinuria decreases | Urea and creatinine every few days | Strict bed rest in complicated cases (e.g. severe hypertension, pulmonary edema) | Salt restriction | Fluid restriction | in oliguric patients: | 1/2 L + volume of previous day urine | Protein restriction | in renal failure: | 0.6–0.8 gm/kg/day | (≈ 40 gm/day for an adult patient) | Monitoring: | Fluid chart (fluid intake and output) and measurement of body weight and blood pressure are part of daily monitoring. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 9

Ch 02 · Acute GN (Nephritic Syndrome) | Treatment — Hypertension, Emergencies & Specific Therapy | e.g. Hypertension & Edema | • Salt restriction | • Diuretics: | loop diuretics | • Antihypertensive drugs — | β-blockers should be used with caution | , as they may precipitate pulmonary edema in patients with impending heart failure. | A. Hypertensive Encephalopathy | Maintain airway | Control blood pressure by parenteral agent, such as | hydralazine 5–20 mg infusion | Control of fits: | IV diazepam (10 mg) | B. Pulmonary Edema / Heart Failure | Salt and water restriction | Ultrafiltration (dialysis) to remove excess fluid in oliguric patient | Acute renal failure: dialysis | Primary GN | Secondary GN | Corticosteroid ± immunosuppressives depending on the histopathological type (see the appropriate section) | Treat the cause, e.g.: PSGN, diabetic nephropathy, Lupus nephritis (see appropriate section) | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 9–10
03 | Nephrotic Syndrome | Definition · Causes · Clinical Features · Investigations · Treatment | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY · Page 10–13

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Definition & Causes | Definition | N.S. is a clinical syndrome characterized by: | 1. Heavy proteinuria | ≥ 3.5 gm/d/1.73 m² body surface area, or urinary protein/creatinine ratio > 3.5 in adults. | 2. Hypoalbuminemia | ≤ 2.5 gm/dl | 3. Edema | 4. Hyperlipidemia | (hypercholesterolemia) | Causes | All causes of acute GN. | Primary: | MCD, MGN, MPGN, MCGN, or FSGN. | Secondary | to: infection, multisystem disease, malignancy, drugs, metabolic or familial causes. | Contrast: | Nephrotic syndrome = | heavy proteinuria | (≥ 3.5 gm/day) with hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia — in contrast to nephritic syndrome where proteinuria is < 3.5 gm/day and hematuria dominates. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 10

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Clinical Features | Proteinuria | 1. Proteinuria: | frothy urine — protein decreases the surface tension of urine, similar to bile salts and detergents. | Edema | 2. Edema: | usually generalized — involves limbs, face, genitalia & serous cavities (ascites, pleural & pericardial effusion). | Severity | of edema correlates with serum albumin & extent of urinary protein losses, and is conditioned by other factors such as heart failure. | Hypertension | 3. Hypertension: | variable, e.g.: | • In | MCD | → blood pressure is | always normal | • In | MCGN | → hypertension is | always present | High-yield: | Frothy urine + generalized edema + hyperlipidemia — think nephrotic syndrome. Remember the MCD vs MCGN blood-pressure contrast. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 10–11

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Investigations — I | Investigation | Finding | 24-h urine protein | 24-h urinary proteins (> 3.5 gm/day in adults) | Plasma proteins | Decreased serum albumin (≤ 2.5 gm/dl). | Serum protein electrophoresis: | decreased albumin; increased alpha2 & beta globulin fractions; normal or slightly increased gamma globulin; increased fibrinogen. | Plasma lipids | Increased cholesterol and LDL. Increased triglycerides in 50% of patients. Normal or decreased HDL (due to increased urinary loss). | Hypocalcemia | Due to urinary loss of cholecalciferol-binding protein. | RFT | Urea, creatinine & eGFR are usually normal. Impaired in: severe hypovolemia → pre-renal AKI; MGN and MCGN. | NB: | in patients with impaired renal function, the biochemical features of NS are uncommon because of the concomitant decrease of GFR. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 11

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Investigations — II & Selective Proteinuria | Investigation | Finding | Urine examination | Red cells and red cell casts → GN (and exclude MCD). | PLA2R | Phospholipase A2 Receptor (PLA2R) antibodies → primary membranous nephropathy (MN). | ↓ Serum C3 | Decreased serum C3 → immune-complex-mediated GN. | ASOT & swab | ASOT & throat swab → streptococcal infection. | ANA / ANCA | ANA → SLE; ANCA → systemic vasculitis. | Hyperglycemia | Hyperglycemia → diabetes mellitus. | Selective Proteinuria | Selective proteinuria | — tested in children. Blood + urine samples are examined simultaneously to determine the clearance of a large-molecular-weight protein (e.g. IgG) in comparison with a small-molecular-weight protein (e.g. albumin or transferrin). | • | Low ratio → selective | proteinuria in MCD, DM & renal amyloidosis | • | High ratio → unselective | proteinuria in crescentic GN | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 11

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Renal Biopsy — Indications & Contraindications | Renal biopsy | Indications: | histological diagnosis and to plan therapy. | In children | Steroid-resistant, steroid-dependent and frequent relapses | Children with renal impairment | In adults | Most adults. | Biopsy NOT indicated in: | • | Young children | with selective proteinuria, normotensive & benign urinary sediment → MCD | • | Long-standing DM | (> 10 years in type 1, > 5 years in type 2) with retinopathy or neuropathy | • | Patients under drug therapy | such as penicillamine | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 11–12

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Treatment — 1. General Treatment | Protein intake | Daily physiological need ( | 1 gm/kg | ) + the daily protein losses in urine. | N.B: | Protein restriction (0.6–0.8 gm/kg/day) in the presence of renal impairment. | High protein intake (1.5–2 gm/kg/day) is NOT advised because: | – Ineffective, due to increased protein loss | – Such a diet is difficult to manage with concomitant salt restriction | – Such a diet could aggravate glomerular damage | Drug control of proteinuria | • | ACE & ARBs: | cause ↓ intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure → ↓ filtered urinary protein losses. | • | Medical nephrectomy | (mercurial drug or renal infarction) to abolish severe persistent proteinuria in ESRD. | Control of Edema | Bed rest → induces diuresis | Na | + | restriction | Diuretics in unresponsive patients | Human albumin infusion: | – | Indications: | severe hypoalbuminemia; diuretic-resistant patient undergoing surgery or an invasive procedure (biopsy) | – | Disadvantages: | expensive & transient effect (24–48 hours) | Rationale | Contrast note: | unlike the general principles chapter, here the emphasis is on replacing losses (albumin) while restricting sodium — never use high-protein diets in nephrotic patients. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 12

Ch 03 · Nephrotic Syndrome | Treatment — Complications & Specific Therapy | Control of complications | Complication | Management | Subnutrition | Proper diet, minerals and vitamins. | N.B: | severe proteinuria may justify ablation of the kidneys by medical or surgical means. | Sepsis | Early detection and aggressive treatment. | Hyperlipidemia | Statins. | Hypertension | Salt restriction + antihypertensives. | Thrombotic complications | Long-term oral anticoagulant. | N.B: | Heparin is ineffective due to concomitant urinary loss of antithrombin III. | N.B: | prophylactic anticoagulant is used in NS due to membranous GN, as thromboembolic complications are common. | In primary N.S. | In secondary N.S. | Depends on the histopathological types — such as MCD, MGN, MCGN, FSGN | Directed to the cause: | • SLE → Steroids + Cyclophosphamide | • DM → Control of hyperglycemia | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 12–13

Ch 04 · Anti-GBM / Goodpasture | Definition, Pathology & Differential Diagnosis | Goodpasture Disease (Anti-GBM GN) | Goodpasture's Syndrome | A | kidney-limited | disease with: | a) GN resulting from glomerular deposition of anti-GBM antibodies | b) Circulating anti-GBM antibodies | A | systemic | disease with a triad of: | a) GN resulting from glomerular deposition of anti-GBM antibodies | b) Circulating anti-GBM antibodies | c) | Pulmonary hemorrhage | Pathology / Histopathology | Diffuse proliferative GN | by LM, and | linear deposits | of anti-GBM IgG antibody by IF. | • G.P. | Disease | → GN | • G.P. | Syndrome | → GN + pulmonary hemorrhage | Differential Diagnosis | D.D. of hemoptysis with renal disease (Pulmonary-Renal Syndromes): | 1. Goodpasture syndrome | 2. Henoch-Schönlein purpura | 3. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) | 4. Microscopic polyangiitis | 5. Cryoglobulinemia | 6. Advanced uremia with pulmonary edema and coagulopathies | 7. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) | 8. Pulmonary embolism with RV thrombosis | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 14

Ch 04 · Anti-GBM / Goodpasture | Investigations & Treatment | Investigations | Evidence of GN: hematuria with dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts and variable degrees of proteinuria | Blood: positive circulating anti-GBM antibodies; other serological tests (complements, ASOT, ANA) are | normal | Renal biopsy: diffuse proliferative GN | Corticosteroids | Cyclophosphamide | IV methylprednisolone | 7–15 mg/kg/day | (maximum 1 gm/day) for | 3 days | , then oral prednisone | 1 mg/kg/day | ; reduce to 20 mg/day by 6 weeks and continue for 6 months. | Dose depends upon the patient’s age: | • < 55 years: 3 mg/kg (down to 50 mg) for 3 months | • > 55 years: 2 mg/kg (down to 50 mg) for 3 months | Plasma exchange | Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis): | replacement with daily | 40–50 ml/kg | plasma with albumin for | 2 weeks | or until anti-GBM antibody disappears. | Caution | N.B.: | Plasmapheresis should | not | be given in patients with anuria and/or crescents > 85% of glomeruli, | unless | there is pulmonary hemorrhage. Albumin is the recommended replacement fluid with plasmapheresis because of the lower incidence of complications. | Protocol: | Summary: | 3 days pulse methylprednisolone → 2 weeks course of daily plasmapheresis → 6 months oral corticosteroids and 3 months cyclophosphamide. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 14–15

Ch 05 · Post-Streptococcal GN | Organism & History of Infection | Organism | Group A | β-hemolytic streptococci | (nephritogenic strains — types | 1, 4, 12, 49 | ). | Type 49 is the most commonly isolated type. | History of streptococcal infection | History of streptococcal infection (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, otitis media, or cellulitis) | 1–2 weeks | before the onset of acute nephritis. | In | skin infection | , the latent period may be prolonged to | 4 weeks | . | The latent period (time between exposure to infection and development of acute nephritis) reflects the time taken for immune-complex formation & deposition and glomerular injury. | N.B.: | A | shorter latent period | signifies exacerbation of underlying CKD (e.g. IgA nephropathy) rather than de novo acute GN. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 15–16

Ch 05 · Post-Streptococcal GN | Clinical Presentation | Presentation | Notes | 1. Acute GN: | in children, picture of acute GN. In adults, the history of streptococcal infection is less commonly obtained, and the onset is subacute or insidious with progressive, slowly developing edema of the lower limbs. | • About 10% of infected individuals develop GN | • Infection may be mild and pass unnoticed | • No relationship between severity of infection and probability of developing acute nephritis | 2. Nephrotic syndrome: | uncommon (< 20% of cases) | 3. RPGN: | in 5% of cases | 4. Asymptomatic: | discovered during routine urine examination | Key points: | ~10% of infected individuals develop GN; the infection may be mild and pass unnoticed, and there is | no relationship | between severity of infection and the probability of developing acute nephritis. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 16

Ch 05 · Post-Streptococcal GN | Investigations | Evidence of streptococcal infection | • Antibodies to streptococcal exo-enzymes: | ASO, DNAase, BNDase and hyaluronidase | • Decrease of | CH50 & C3 | during the acute phase, then returns to normal within | 8 weeks | of nephritis (transient hypocomplementemia) | Evidence of acute GN | Modality | Finding | Urine examination | Dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts & proteinuria (< 3 gm/day) | Blood | Transient increase of serum cholesterol (in NS), decreased serum albumin, renal impairment | Renal biopsy — LM | Diffuse endocapillary proliferative GN ± few crescents | Renal biopsy — EM | Subepithelial electron-dense deposits ( | humps | ) and variable degrees of mesangial deposits | Renal biopsy — IF | Granular deposits of C3 & IgG | Biopsy triad: | Subepithelial humps | on EM + | granular C3 & IgG | on IF + | transient low C3 (recovers < 8 weeks) | → PSGN. | PRINCIPLES OF NEPHROLOGY — Page 16–17

Ch 05 · Post-Streptococcal GN | Treatment | General / Supportive / Symptomatic | Bed rest | Diet: salt, fluid and protein restriction | Drugs: | a. Diuretics | b. Vasodilators for control of blood pressure | c. Steroids, cytotoxic drugs and anticoagulants are | of no value | and may be harmful — | except in RPGN | Dialysis for renal failure | Specific treatment | Antibiotic (penicillin) therapy. | For patients | For close contacts | Aim: | • Decrease antigen load → decrease immune-complex formation → may stop progression of disease | • Halt spread of potentially nephritogenic streptococci from the patient to family members in close contact | • Such treatment, however, does | not | seem to be very effective in aborting or ameliorating the course of the disease | Use of short-term penicillin prophylaxis ( | phenoxy penicillin 500 mg/day | ) to all individuals at high risk in a closed community or family. | N.B.: | No effect of long-term penicillin in prophylaxis after the development of GN. Removal of infected tonsils or septic foci should be delayed until convalescence is advanced, as the operation may be followed by exacerbation of the disease. However, if needed, give benzyl penicillin on the day of operation and for three days after.

Drugs | Statins and lipid-lowering drugs. | Cocaine. | Amphetamine derivatives. | 7. Infectious diseases | Viral: | Coxsackie, HIV, Influenza. | Bacterial: | Clostridia infection, Legionella, Streptococcal infection, Staphylococcal infection, Pneumococcal pneumonia. | 8. Toxins | Snake venom, poisonous mushrooms, fish poisoning ( | Haff disease | ). | 9. Miscellaneous | Malignant hyperthermia | , | neuroleptic malignant syndrome | .

3 | Rhabdomyolysis — Pathogenesis | Mild and moderate rhabdomyolysis | (e.g. after intense exertion, violent repetitive activities or a grand mal seizure) → | direct injury of muscle cells and depletion of energy stores | → muscle pain and weakness. | Severe acute rhabdomyolysis (crush injury / pigmented nephropathy) | AKI is due to; | 1. Renal ischemia: | Myoglobin has | intense vasoconstrictive effect | → renal ischemia. | 2. Tubular obstruction and injury: | Once the myoglobin molecule is filtered by the glomerulus and enters the PCT fluid; | a. A portion enters the | PCT cells | ; inside the cells the molecule releases | elemental iron and iron compounds | forming toxic products that injure the cells. | b. The remaining unabsorbed pigment passes to the | distal nephron | and interacts with | Tamm-Horsfall protein | (in | acidic urine | ) forming a | gel | and obstructing urine flow. Then the concentration of pigment in the tubule rises, augmenting proximal tubular absorption and toxicity.

3 | Rhabdomyolysis — Diagnosis | Clinical features | Depend on the severity of muscle injury. | Mild and moderate cases: | muscular pain, tenderness, edema, stiffness, weakness and impaired mobility. | Severe acute cases (crush injury): AKI. | Laboratory | Estimation of serum | Creatine Kinase “CK” | enzyme level; | Elevated total serum CK levels | > 500 IU/L | → | high suspicion | of acute rhabdomyolysis. | The | CK-MM isoform | → the | most sensitive test | to confirm the diagnosis.

3 | Rhabdomyolysis — Treatment & Prognosis | Treatment | Severe cases should be managed in ICU. | Aggressive and urgent volume replacement | to maintain organ perfusion — | caution | must be taken to avoid volume overload and pulmonary edema. | Alkalinization of urine | with bicarb infusion to prevent obstructive cast formation. | Special care to | respiratory failure | due to diaphragmatic weakness if severe. | Monitor for | hyperkalemia | by ECG and serum potassium level. | Dialysis for severe AKI. | Prognosis | Those who survive acute rhabdomyolysis are at risk of | permanent disability (muscle fibrosis) | .

01 | Chronic Kidney Disease | Definitions · Markers · Grades · Causes · Clinical Picture · Investigations · Treatment

Definitions | CKD | is defined as | abnormalities of kidney structure or function, present for > 3 months | with implications for health, and is classified based on | cause, GFR category and albuminuria category | . | Chronic Renal Failure (CRF): | GFR is | < 60 ml/min/1.73 m² for ≥ 3 months | (Grade 3 CKD). | End Stage Renal Disease (ESRD): | a | permanent and irreversible renal impairment | which | necessitates renal replacement therapy | = Grade 5 CKD.

Markers of Kidney Damage | Functional Markers | Albuminuria: | albumin excretion rate (AER) ≥ 30 mg/24 h, or albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) ≥ 30 mg/g. | Urine sediment abnormalities. | Electrolytes and other abnormalities | due to tubular disorders. | Structural Markers | Structural abnormalities detected by histology. | Structural abnormalities detected by imaging. | History of kidney transplantation.

Grades (Stages) of CKD | Classified according to GFR category (five grades) and albuminuria category (3 grades). | Grade | GFR (ml/min/1.73 m²) | Terms | G1 | ≥ 90 | Normal or high | G2 | 60 – 89 | Mildly decreased* | G3a | 45 – 89 | Mildly to moderately decreased | G3b | 30 – 44 | Moderately to severely decreased | G4 | 15 – 29 | Severely decreased | G5 | < 15 | ESRD | NB: | In the absence of evidence of kidney damage, neither GFR category G1 nor G2 fulfill the criteria for CKD. *Relative to young adult level.

Albuminuria Categories in CKD | Category | AER (mg/24 h) | ACR (mg/g) | Terms | A1 | < 30 | < 30 | Normal to mildly increased | A2 | 30 – 300 | 30 – 300 | Moderately increased* | A3 | > 300 | > 300 | Severely increased** | NB: | **Including nephrotic syndrome (albumin excretion usually > 2200 mg/24 h & ACR > 2200 mg/g). *Relative to young adult level.

Causes of CKD | 1. | Diabetes mellitus. | 2. | Hypertension. | 3. | Glomerulopathies, either primary or secondary. | 4. | Tubulo-interstitial diseases. | 5. | Renal vascular diseases (renal artery stenosis). | 6. | Hereditary renal diseases e.g. PCKD, Alport’s syndrome, oxalosis. | 7. | Obstructive uropathy e.g. urolithiasis, prostatic enlargement, tumors, retroperitoneal fibrosis. | 8. | Recurrent UTI (pyelonephritis, vesicoureteral reflux). | 9. | Drugs and toxins; NSAID, chronic lead poisoning. | 10. | Uncertain (in up to 15% of cases).

Diagnosis — Clinical Features (GIT) | Overview: | CKD leads to disturbances in the function of every system in the body. The presentation and severity vary greatly from patient to patient depending on the grade/severity of disease. | Grades 1–3 are usually asymptomatic; Grades 4 & 5 are symptomatic. | Gastrointestinal | 1. | Anorexia, nausea, vomiting & hiccough (early & controlled by protein restriction). | 2. | Uremic fetor; uriniferous odor of breath (breakdown of urea to ammonia). | 3. | Mucosal ulcerations (in late stages) → GIT bleeding. | 4. | Peptic ulcer; increased gastric acidity, gastrin secretion, secondary hyperparathyroidism. | 5. | Increased incidence of diverticulosis (in patients with PCKD). | NB: | GIT symptoms are improved by dialysis, except peptic ulcers and diverticulosis.

Clinical Features — Cardiovascular | Cardiovascular | 1. | CHF and pulmonary edema; dyspnea, orthopnea, increased jugular venous pressure, lower limb edema due to volume overload. | 2. | Arrhythmias; due to electrolyte abnormalities. | 3. | Hypertension. | 4. | Pericarditis and pericardial effusion. | 5. | Accelerated atherosclerosis. | NB: | Absence of hypertension in a CKD patient may be due to: salt wasting nephropathy e.g. PCKD · use of anti-hypertensive drugs · volume depletion e.g. GIT loss or diuretic overdose.

Clinical Features — Respiratory & Hematological | Respiratory | Acidotic breathing. | Pleurisy. | Chest infection. | Hematological — Anemia | Anemia | → easy fatigability, palpitation & tachycardia, due to: | Erythropoietin deficiency. | Decreased life span of RBCs and toxic bone marrow suppression. | Decreased nutrient intake and absorption; iron, vitamin B12, folate. | Bleeding tendency. | Secondary hyperparathyroidism. | Chronic inflammation. | Blood loss during dialysis and from GIT.

Clinical Features — Hematological (cont.) | Bleeding Diathesis | Due to: prolongation of bleeding time, decreased factor III activity, abnormal platelet aggregation and adhesion, and impaired prothrombin consumption. | Enhanced Susceptibility to Infection | Impaired leukocyte formation and function | due to: acidosis, hyperglycemia, hyperosmolarity of serum and tissues by azotemia, and malnutrition. | Defective mucosal barriers. | Use of steroids and immunosuppressive drugs.

Clinical Features — Endocrine & Metabolism | 1. | Insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance. | 2. | Decreased insulin metabolism and degradation by the diseased kidney → decreased insulin requirement for diabetic patients. | 3. | Thyroid dysfunction; increased TRH → release of prolactin with impaired prolactin clearance → galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and impotence. | 4. | Hypocalcemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism. | 5. | Decreased serum testosterone level → impotence, decreased spermatogenesis and infertility. | 6. | Menstrual abnormalities (oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea) and infertility.

Bone — CKD-MBD: Definition & Pathophysiology | Definition of CKD-MBD | A systemic disorder of mineral and bone metabolism due to CKD, manifested by one or a combination of: | 1. | Abnormalities of calcium, phosphorus, PTH, or vitamin D metabolism. | 2. | Abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth or strength (renal osteodystrophy). | 3. | Vascular or other soft tissue calcification e.g. cardiac valve, arterial calcification and calciphylaxis. | Pathophysiology (Figure 10, Martin et al., 2007) | 1. | Reduction of GFR < 60 ml/min → decreased phosphorus filtration → hyperphosphatemia → PTH secretion stimulation. | 2. | Decreased renal production of 1α-hydroxylase → decreased active vitamin D3 “1,25(OH)₂ vit. D” → hypocalcemia → in addition to hyperphosphatemia → secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT).

PTH mRNA stability | Above “Hypocalcemia” | ↑ Phosphorus, ↓ Calcitriol, Calcitriol Resistance, Skeletal Resistance | Below “↓ Calcitriol” | ↑ Phosphorus, ↓ Renal Mass, ? ↓ 25(OH)D, ? ↓ 1-25, ? acidosis, ? other | Below “Skeletal Resistance” | ↑ Phosphorus, Desens. to PTH, ? ↓ PTH-R, ↓ calcitriol, ? Uremic toxins, ? PTH inhibitors

Renal Osteodystrophy — Definition & Types | Definition: | the skeletal component of the systemic disorder of MBD that occurs in patients with CKD. Patients may suffer from; bone pain, pathological (spontaneous) fractures, and bone changes in bone imaging and bone biopsy. | It includes (Figure 11): | 1. | Osteitis fibrosa (high turnover bone disease): | a manifestation of hyperparathyroidism characterized by increased osteoclast and osteoblast activity (turnover) and peritrabecular fibrosis. | 2. | Osteomalacia: | a condition characterized by abnormally low bone turnover. | 3. | Adynamic bone disease: | decreased rates of bone formation with normal bone mineralization; due to aggressive suppression of PTH leading to hypoparathyroidism. | 4. | Osteopenia or osteoporosis: | increased skeletal fragility as a result of reduced bone quantity and quality. | 5. | Mixed lesions: | combination of these abnormalities; high PTH levels + impaired bone formation and mineralization. Usually seen in patients with previously established hyperparathyroid bone disease who develop aluminum-related bone disease.

Figure 11 — Spectrum of Renal Osteodystrophy | Figure 11 — Skeletal abnormalities in renal bone disease (spectrum of renal osteodystrophy; Martin et al., 2015): | Adynamic bone / Osteomalacia | Low turnover | → | Normal | → | Mild | → | Osteitis fibrosa | High turnover — Hyperparathyroidism | Mixed | (between Adynamic/Osteomalacia and Osteitis fibrosa) | Below the spectrum: | Calcium, calcitriol and Aluminum

Clinical Features — Neurological | CNS | Early: | inability to concentrate, loss of memory, drowsiness, insomnia, hiccups, cramps and muscle twitching. | Late: | asterixis, myoclonus, chorea, stupor, seizures and coma. | Peripheral Nerves | Sensory (early) and motor neuropathy. | Restless legs syndrome: | discomfort in the feet and legs with frequent leg movement. | Treatment: | early dialysis or transplantation. | In Dialysis Patients | Dialysis dementia (encephalopathy). | Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: | (nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, headache, seizures). Occurs in the first few sessions of dialysis; due to rapid removal of urea with rapid reduction of osmolality of the extracellular compartment within the cranium → cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure.

Clinical Features — Dermatological | 1. | Earthy (muddy) face due to combination of anemia and retention of urochrome pigment. | 2. | Pallor due to anemia. | 3. | Ecchymosis and hematomas due to defective hemostasis. | 4. | Pruritus due to calcium deposition and secondary hyperparathyroidism. | 5. | Poor skin turgor and dry mucous membranes due to dehydration. | 6. | Evidence of malnutrition. | 7. | Uremic frost (in advanced cases); a fine white powder due to high urea concentration in sweat which precipitates on skin after evaporation. | 8. | Slate-gray-bronze discoloration of skin (hemochromatosis) due to multiple blood transfusions in dialysis patients. | 9. | Half and half nails. | 10. | Calciphylaxis (calcific uremic arteriolopathy): vascular calcification of skin, muscles and subcutaneous tissues. The skin shows violaceous rashes, nonhealing ulcers, and gangrene → high mortality. | NB: | Most skin abnormalities improve with dialysis, except pruritus which persists.

Clinical Features — Urinary & Electrolytes | Urinary System | UTI. | Urine volume: | Early; polyuria and nocturia. | Late; oliguria and anuria. | Electrolytes & Acid-Base Disturbances | 1. | Hyperkalemia → muscle weakness, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest. | 2. | Hypocalcemia → tetany is rare as acidosis increases ionized calcium. | 3. | Hyperphosphatemia → itching, metastatic calcification. | 4. | Metabolic acidosis → rapid deep breathing, convulsions.

Investigations — Part A | A. To establish the degree of renal impairment and complications | 2. Investigations | 1. | Urine analysis with evaluation of albuminuria, broad casts, and low fixed specific gravity. | 2. | Kidney function tests; urea, creatinine and eGFR. | 3. | Serum electrolytes: Sodium, Potassium, Calcium and Phosphorus. | 4. | Arterial blood gases. | 5. | Serum uric acid. | 6. | Complete blood count. | 7. | Iron profile. | 8. | iPTH level. | 9. | Skeletal survey.

Investigations — Part B | B. To determine the underlying disease (if the cause is not clear) | 2. Investigations | 1. | Serum and urine protein electrophoresis. | 2. | ANA, anti-ds DNA ab, C3 & C4, ANCA, AGBM ab. | 3. | Hepatitis C and B and HIV serology. | 4. | Renal imaging: kidney ureter bladder X-ray (KUB), ultrasound, CT, MRI, radionuclide scan (renogram). | 5. | Renal biopsy: | not indicated | if there is a small atrophic kidney.

Investigations — Part C | C. To diagnose a patient with acute RF on top of CKD | 2. Investigations | 1. | Bone disease. | 2. | Uremic neuropathy. | 3. | Profound anemia, hyperphosphatemia, and high serum creatinine with mild symptoms. | 4. | Small sized kidney | except in; | DM, amyloidosis, multiple myeloma and PCKD. | NB: | Part C — the listed features suggest chronicity (CKD) rather than acute kidney injury.

Treatment — Conservative (Overview) | I) Conservative treatment includes: | 1. Correction of any reversible cause and underlying disease · 2. Control of symptoms · 3. Educational programs to the patients and their relatives | Correction of Any Reversible Cause (to delay CKD progression) | 1. | Good blood glucose control. | 2. | Good blood pressure control. | 3. | Good hydration. | 4. | Correction of renal obstruction and UTI. | 5. | Treatment of active primary renal disease. | 6. | Treatment of sepsis. | 7. | Reduction of proteinuria (ACEI/ARBs, avoid combination). | 8. | Control of dyslipidemia. | 9. | Lifestyle modification (diet, weight reduction, smoking & alcohol cessation, exercise). | 10. | Avoid nephrotoxins and large doses of contrast agents.

Control of Symptoms — Diet & GIT | Diet (low protein, potassium, phosphate, and salts) + fluid balance | 1. | Low protein diet (0.6–0.8 gm/kg/day). Protein diet should be increased when the patient starts dialysis. | 2. | Low potassium diet (if the patient is hypokalemic, increase potassium diet). | 3. | Low phosphate diet. | 4. | Salt restriction (free salt intake in salt-losing nephropathy). | 5. | Fluid balance; depends on urine output. | GIT | 1. | Hiccough and vomiting → prokinetics. If persist → dialysis. | 2. | Gastritis; proton pump inhibitors (avoid long term use as may cause interstitial nephropathy).

Control of Symptoms — Cardiovascular | 1. | Control of hypertension; ACEI/ARBs, CCB, BB. | 2. | ACEI or ARBs are preferred if there is proteinuria, but with careful monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium levels. | 3. | Volume overload → loop diuretics. | 4. | Pericarditis → dialysis.

Treatment — Mineral Bone Disease (1) | Mineral Bone Disease (MBD) — Control of hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, vitamin D deficiency and secondary hyperparathyroidism | Diet Control | 1. | Increased elementary dietary calcium to 1500–2000 mg/day (hold if there is hypercalcemia). | 2. | Low phosphate diet (800–1000 mg/day) adjusted by requirement of protein in grades 3–5 CKD patients. | Phosphate Binders — indicated when dietary phosphate restriction is insufficient to control phosphate and PTH levels | Calcium-based phosphate binders; | e.g. Ca carbonate, given orally during meals. | A. Decreases serum phosphate level effectively and can be used for initial phosphate binding treatment. | B. Long-term administration can result in hypercalcemia. | C. Should not be used in dialysis patients with hypercalcemia and in patients with plasma PTH level < 130 pg/dL. In these conditions use calcium-free phosphate binders. | Non-calcium-based phosphate binders; | Sevelamer (Renagel) hydrochloride or bicarbonate — safe and effective but expensive. | Lanthanum carbonate.

Treatment — Mineral Bone Disease (2) | Calcimimetic agents (cinacalcet) | — inhibits iPTH secretion. | Vitamin D analogs (alfacalcidol/calcitriol; 0.25–2 µg daily) | according to serum Ca, PO₄ and iPTH levels. | Hold if there is hypercalcemia and/or hyperphosphatemia. | Treatment with vitamin D is recommended for renal patients with: | 1. | Total serum calcium level < 9.5 mg/dl. | 2. | Serum phosphate level < 4.6 mg/dl. | 3. | Elevated serum PTH level. | Parathyroidectomy | in severe hyperparathyroidism (PTH > 800 pg/dL) not responding to medications.

Treatment — Anemia & Pruritus | Management of Anemia | 1. | Iron therapy: oral in pre-dialysis patients and better I.V. for HD patients. | 2. | Erythropoietin; subcutaneous or intravenous: | • Erythropoietin alpha or beta. | • Long acting darbepoetin alfa. | • Continuous erythropoiesis receptor activator (CERA). | Pruritus | 1. | Moistening ointment. | 2. | Gabapentin, Naltrexone. | 3. | Short wave ultraviolet. | 4. | Increase dose of dialysis.

Treatment — Educational Program & RRT | Correction of electrolyte and acid-base disorders — see Chapter V (Electrolytes & Acid-Base). | Educational Program | Explain the possibility of eventual renal failure and forms of therapy. | Patients planning for HD | → preparation of A-V fistula. | Patients planning for PD or transplantation | → early education of family members for selection and preparation of a home dialysis helper or a related donor. | II) Renal Replacement Therapy | Dialysis and renal transplantation.
02 | Renal Replacement Therapy | Dialysis (Peritoneal & Hemodialysis) · Kidney Transplantation

RRT — Overview & Definition of Dialysis | Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT) | Dialysis (Peritoneal and hemodialysis). | Renal transplantation. | Dialysis — Definition | A process of diffusion of substances and water across a semipermeable membrane in both directions (blood on one side and fluid “dialysate” on the other side of the membrane).

Indications of Dialysis | I) Temporary (acute / urgent) dialysis | 1. | In AKI: many nephrologists advise early dialysis in AKI in all patients, at least for some periods of time, to simplify management which enhances recovery and minimizes development of complications. | 2. | Control of some uremic symptoms and complications (in both AKI and CKD) as: | • Refractory hyperkalemia. | • Intractable metabolic acidosis. | • Progressive fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics. | • Pericarditis and pleuritis. | • CNS complications. | • GIT complications. | • Bleeding due to uremia. | 3. | Removal of dialyzable toxins & drugs as; alcohols, aspirin, lithium, contrast dyes. | II) Permanent (chronic, regular or maintenance) dialysis | Grade 5 CKD (ESRD) as replacement therapy when GFR ≤ 10 ml/min, which may correspond to a serum creatinine of 8–10 mg/dL.

Dialysis — Contraindications & Types | Contraindications | Refractory hypotension unresponsive to vasopressors. | Terminal illness. | Organic brain damage. | Types | Peritoneal dialysis (PD). | Hemodialysis (HD).

Peritoneal Dialysis — Principles & Indications | Principles | Utilizes the peritoneal membrane (with its capillaries) as a semipermeable membrane. | When fluid is introduced into the peritoneal cavity it equilibrates with the extracellular fluid. | Removal of the introduced fluid (effluent) results in removal of waste products (solutes) and excess fluid from the body. | Indications — all patients with symptomatic uremia; specific indications: | 1. | A slowly rising urea. | 2. | Patients with cardiovascular or hemodynamic instability. | 3. | Absence of H.D. facilities. | 4. | Patients with immature A-V fistula. | 5. | Poor vascular access. | 6. | High risk of anticoagulation in a dialysis dependent patient.

Peritoneal Dialysis — Contraindications | Absolute Contraindications | 1. | Peritoneal fibrosis (> 50%) — inadequate peritoneal surface area for dialysis. | 2. | Pleuro-peritoneal leak → hydrothorax. | 3. | Multiple large abdominal wounds with drains. | Relative Contraindications | 1. | Abdominal problems; colostomy, nephrostomy, recent abdominal or thoracic surgery, extensive abdominal adhesions, hernia, abdominal malignancy. | 2. | Severe hypercatabolic states e.g. burn. | 3. | Fresh or infected aortic prosthesis. | 4. | Huge polycystic kidneys (insufficient intraperitoneal space). | 5. | Active diverticulosis. | 6. | Morbid obesity (inadequate clearance). | 7. | Hyperlipidemia. | 8. | Severe gastroparesis (worsening vomiting). | 9. | For self-care (home dialysis) patient.

Peritoneal Dialysis — Advantages | 1. | Safe and easy to perform. | 2. | Preserves residual renal function. | 3. | No routine anticoagulation. | 4. | Avoidance of vascular surgery. | 5. | Slow clearance rate → fewer dialysis-related symptoms e.g. disequilibrium or hypotension. | 6. | Better control of PTH. | 7. | More liberal diet. | 8. | Fewer medications. | 9. | Less expensive than HD. | 10. | Less risk of transmission of blood-borne viruses.

Peritoneal Dialysis — Disadvantages & Complications (1) | Disadvantages | 1. | Long time. | 2. | Low efficiency. | 3. | Inadequate clearance in some patients e.g. malignant hypertension, peritoneal disease, vasculitis. | 4. | Contraindicated in recent abdominal surgery or pulmonary compromise. | 5. | Associated complications. | Complications (1–6) | 1. | Peritonitis. | 2. | Catheter exit site infection. | 3. | Constipation. | 4. | Leakage of dialysate through a diaphragmatic defect into the thoracic cavity → massive pleural effusion and respiratory embarrassment, or to the scrotum. | 5. | Failure of peritoneal membrane function → ultrafiltration failure. | 6. | Sclerosing peritonitis (rare but potentially fatal).

Peritoneal Dialysis — Complications (2) | 7. | Moderate protein loss → malnutrition. | 8. | Hyperlipidemia → accelerated atherosclerosis. | 9. | Obesity due to mobilization of glucose from the dialysate to the body. | 10. | Inguinal and abdominal hernias. | 11. | Traumatic perforation of an abdominal organ (bowel, bladder, blood vessel). | 12. | Clotting of the cannula.

Hemodialysis — Definition & Advantages | Definition | A process of diffusion across a semipermeable membrane, to remove unwanted substances from blood while adding desirable components. | Advantages of HD | 1. | Relatively short time, causing minimal interruption of lifestyle between treatments. | 2. | More efficient than PD. | 3. | Can be performed in the home.

HD — Surgical Complications (Vascular Access) | Of Catheters | Bleeding. | Infection. | Thrombosis or stenosis of the vessels. | Pneumothorax. | Air embolism. | Of A-V Fistula and of Graft | 1. | Stenosis → inadequate blood flow. | 2. | Thrombosis. | 3. | Infection. | 4. | Failure to develop adequate venous outflow. | 5. | Vascular steal → limb ischemia. | 6. | Venous hypertension syndrome (distal venous stasis → skin necrosis). | 7. | High output heart failure. | 8. | Pseudo-aneurysms.

HD — Acute Medical Complications | 1. | Intradialytic hypotension (IDH). | 2. | Hypertension. | 3. | Cramps. | 4. | Nausea and vomiting. | 5. | Headache. | 6. | Fever. | 7. | Hemolysis: rare, but potentially serious. | 8. | Bleeding: anticoagulant overdose. | 9. | Clotting of extracorporeal circuit (blood lines and dialyzer). | 10. | Chest pain. | 11. | Arrhythmias. | 12. | Cardiac arrest in the dialysis unit. | 13. | Air embolism. | 14. | Disequilibrium syndrome.

HD — Chronic Complications (1): Cardiovascular | Chronic (Long-term) HD Complications — 1. Cardiovascular Disease | Dialysis patients are more likely to die from CV disease than the general population. The cause is multifactorial; cardiac or vascular. | Cardiac | Ischemic heart disease. | Valvular heart disease (aortic and mitral valves). | Uremic pericarditis and pericardial effusion. | Uremic endocarditis. | Cardiomyopathy (dilated). | Vascular | Peripheral vascular disease | due to: | • Decreased peripheral blood flow, related to vascular access. | • Hypertension and dyslipidemia. | Metastatic calcification: | abnormal calcification of soft tissues due to persistent elevation of plasma phosphate and calcium.

HD — Chronic Complications (2) | Neuropsychiatric, Nutrition & Bone | Neuropsychiatric complications: | anxiety, depression, dementia. | Malnutrition. | Dialysis osteomalacia. | Dialysis related amyloidosis (DRA). | Rheumatologic & Other | Rheumatologic complications: | • Crystal-induced arthritis. | • Infection of joints and bone. | • Ischemic necrosis of bone. | Hypersplenism. | Acquired renal cystic disease: | • In patients with prolonged dialysis > 3 years. | • May show malignant changes.

Kidney Transplantation — Definition, Donors & Contraindications | Definition | Surgical implantation of a kidney obtained from either a healthy kidney donor or a brain stem dead cadaver (deceased). | Types of Donors | Living (blood related, unrelated) donor. | Deceased (cadaveric) donor. | Contraindications | 1. | Patient’s refusal. | 2. | Psychosis. | 3. | Elderly (relative contraindication). | 4. | Active sepsis. | 5. | Unstable cardiovascular disease. | 6. | Severe respiratory distress. | 7. | Cerebro-vascular hemorrhage. | 8. | Advanced liver disease; unless combined liver and kidney transplantation. | 9. | Malignancies. | 10. | Un-repairable urological abnormalities.

Transplantation — Common Complications | Surgical Complications | 1. | Technical failures. | 2. | Renal vein and renal artery thrombosis. | 3. | Urine leakage at uretero-vesical anastomosis. | 4. | Leg edema (lymphedema) on the same side of the implanted kidney. | Medical Complications | 1. | Acute tubular necrosis (ATN). | 2. | Rejection (hyperacute, acute, chronic). | 3. | Complications of immunosuppression. | 4. | Recurrence of the primary renal disease. | 5. | Infection (opportunistic). | 6. | Malignancy (Kaposi sarcoma of the skin, lymphoproliferative). | 7. | Hypertension, DM, atherosclerosis, bone disease. | 8. | GIT bleeding, cataract, bone marrow suppression. | 9. | Nephrotoxicity and hepatotoxicity.

Summary | CKD Essentials | Structure/function abnormalities > 3 months. | Classified by cause + GFR (G1–G5) + albuminuria (A1–A3). | ESRD = Grade 5 = needs RRT. | Clinical Picture | GIT: anorexia, vomiting, uremic fetor. | CVS: CHF, HTN, pericarditis, atherosclerosis. | Hematological: anemia, bleeding, infections. | Bone: CKD-MBD & renal osteodystrophy. | Neuro, skin, urinary & electrolyte disturbances. | Investigations | Urine analysis, KFT (urea, creatinine, eGFR), electrolytes, A#F1E8D9. | Iron profile, iPTH, skeletal survey. | Serology, renal imaging, biopsy (not if small atrophic kidneys). | Conservative Treatment | Correct reversible causes & underlying disease. | Control BP, glucose, proteinuria (ACEI/ARBs), lipids, lifestyle. | Diet, GIT, CVS, MBD, anemia & pruritus management. | Educational programs. | Dialysis | PD: peritoneum as membrane; safe, preserves residual function. | HD: efficient, short time; vascular-access surgical complications + acute/chronic medical complications. | Indications: AKI, uremic complications, toxins, ESRD (GFR ≤ 10). | Transplantation | Living or deceased donor. | Contraindications: refusal, psychosis, sepsis, malignancy, etc. | Complications: rejection, immunosuppression, infection, malignancy.

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Definition & The Anion Gap | Definition | Decrease in | blood pH | due to a decrease in | serum HCO | 3 | − | concentrations. | The Anion Gap (AG) | Plasma is | electro-neutral | , i.e. total anions match total cations. | The major | measured | plasma cation is | Na | + | ; the major | measured | anions are | HCO | 3 | − | and | Cl | − | . | There are | unmeasured | plasma cations (e.g. K | + | , Mg | 2+ | and Ca | 2+ | ) as well as | unmeasured | anions (e.g. sulfate, phosphate and some organic anions). | The unmeasured anions are | slightly more | than the unmeasured cations; this difference is termed | "the Anion Gap (AG)" | . | Based on the fact that the total cations equal the total anions; AG can be calculated as the difference between the major cation (Na | + | ) and the sum of the major anions (HCO | 3 | − | and Cl | − | ), i.e. | AG = Na | + | − (HCO | 3 | − | + Cl | − | ) | . | NB: | An | increase of AG | can result from either: a | decrease in the unmeasured cations | (e.g. hypokalemia) or an | increase in the unmeasured anions | (e.g. hyperphosphatemia).

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Anion Gap: Formula & Types | AG formula | AG = Na | + | − (HCO | 3 | − | + Cl | − | ) | In certain forms of metabolic acidosis, acidic substances (anions) accumulate and increase the AG | Why the AG matters | By recognizing the | increase in the AG | , this can help to | differentiate the cause | of acidosis. Thus, metabolic acidosis can be either: | 1. High AG metabolic acidosis | The reduction in plasma HCO | 3 | − | equals | the increase in AG. | 2. Normal (Non) AG metabolic acidosis | The reduction in plasma HCO | 3 | − | is compensated by an | increase in plasma Cl | − | to maintain electro-neutrality ( | hyperchloremic | metabolic acidosis). | ⚠ Important: | High AG: the “extra” unmeasured anions are the retained acids. Normal AG: chloride rises to balance the lost bicarbonate (hyperchloremic).

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Causes & Classification | Normal AG (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis | GI loss of HCO | 3 | − | (e.g. | diarrhea | , enteric fistula). | Renal loss of HCO | 3 | − | ( | Proximal Type II RTA | ). | Failure of renal H | + | secretion ( | Distal Type I RTA | ). | Acid infusion (e.g. | ammonium chloride | , hyperalimentation). | High AG metabolic acidosis | Ketoacidosis | (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). | Renal failure | (phosphate, sulfate, urate). | Lactic acidosis | (L-lactate, D-lactate). | Massive rhabdomyolysis | (H | + | and organic anions from the damaged muscles). | Exogenous | (salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol, metformin). | NB: | Mnemonics of high AG acidosis: | K.U.S.M.A.U.L. | -like list — | K | etoacidosis, | U | remia (renal failure), | S | alicylates, | M | ethanol, | A | lcohol (ketoacidosis), | U | ric acid (rhabdomyolysis), | L | actic acidosis.

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Clinical Features | Symptoms | Variable degrees of | dyspnea | (due to hyperventilation). | Other symptoms are | non-specific | and symptoms of the cause if present, e.g.; | 1- Symptoms of | diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) | or of | CKD | . | 2- History of | alcoholism | , drug intake (e.g. salicylates, acetazolamide, metformin), or of | renal stone | (e.g. in RTA). | Signs | The most prominent sign is | Kussmaul Respiration | (rapid deep breathing). | Other signs are non-specific if present, e.g.; | 1- | Hypotension | , cardiac arrhythmia. | 2- | Disturbed consciousness | and coma. | 3- Signs of the cause, e.g. DKA, CKD, or alcoholism. | Key examination point | Kussmaul respiration | (rapid, deep sighing breathing) is the hallmark respiratory sign — the body attempts to blow off CO | 2 | to compensate the metabolic acidosis.

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Investigations | General investigations | → to diagnose metabolic acidosis and calculate AG, e.g.; | ABG | (arterial blood gases): pH, HCO | 3 | − | , CO | 2 | Serum electrolytes | : Na | + | , K | + | and Cl | − | Specific investigations | → to diagnose the etiology, e.g.; | Kidney functions | Blood glucose level | Urinary ketones | Serum lactate | Toxicological screening | NB: | Stepwise approach: | confirm acidosis on ABG (low pH + low HCO | 3 | − | ) → compute the AG from electrolytes → then target specific tests according to the suspected etiology.

1A | Metabolic Acidosis — Treatment | General principles | Treatment is generally directed to the | underlying condition or disease | . | Treatment of acidosis using | alkali therapy (HCO | 3 | − | ) | is usually indicated to raise plasma pH above | 7.20 | in the following circumstances: | 1. Low HCO | 3 | − | + PCO | 2 | near compensation limit | Low serum HCO | 3 | − | and PCO | 2 | close to the lower limit of compensation (approximately | 15 mmHg | ). Any further drop in HCO | 3 | − | will not be matched by a corresponding fall in PCO | 2 | → | marked drop in pH | . | 2. Well-compensated acidosis + impending respiratory failure | Well-compensated metabolic acidosis with | impending respiratory failure | due to respiratory muscle fatigue. PCO | 2 | starts to rise → | dramatic drop in pH | . | Route of administration of bicarbonate | I.V. sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO | 3 | ) | : corrects | acute | metabolic acidosis. Deficit can be calculated as: | (Desired HCO | 3 | − | − Measured HCO | 3 | − | ) × 0.5 × body weight | . | Oral sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO | 3 | ) | : used to correct | chronic | metabolic acidosis (e.g. RTA) and uncommonly used in acute situations when the I.V. route is not suitable. | Monitoring: | serum HCO | 3 | − | and pH should be assessed frequently; monitor serum Na | + | , volume status and PCO | 2 | during treatment.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Definition & Classification | Definition | An increase in | blood pH | due to increase in | serum HCO | 3 | − | concentrations. | Causes and classification | Causes of metabolic alkalosis can be classified into; | 1. Chloride-responsive | urine chloride | < 20 mEq/L | 2. Chloride-resistant | urine chloride | > 20 mEq/L | 3. Other causes | including | alkali-loading | alkalosis | NB: | The | urine chloride | measurement is the key first step — it separates saline-responsive from saline-resistant alkalosis.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Causes (Chloride-responsive & Other) | A. Causes of chloride-responsive alkalosis (urine chloride < 20 mEq/L) | Loss of gastric secretions | ; vomiting, nasogastric suction. | Loss of colonic secretions | ; congenital chloridorrhea, villous adenoma. | Volume depletion. | Thiazides and loop diuretics | (after discontinuation). | Cystic fibrosis. | C. Other causes of metabolic alkalosis | Exogenous alkali administration: | sodium bicarbonate | or | massive blood transfusion | (high citrate content) in the presence of renal insufficiency. | Recovery of metabolic acidosis | (due to the metabolism of lactic acid or ketoacids). | Milk-alkali syndrome | (comprises hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and metabolic alkalosis). | Hypercalcemia | causes volume depletion and enhanced bicarbonate reabsorption. | Hypoalbuminemia | : may be related to loss of negative charges of albumin.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Causes (Chloride-resistant) | B1. Chloride-resistant with hypertension | Hyperaldosteronism | (primary, adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma, glucocorticoid-remediable hyperaldosteronism). | Cushing syndrome. | Exogenous steroids. | Liddle’s syndrome. | Reno-vascular hypertension. | B2. Chloride-resistant without hypertension | Bartter’s syndrome. | Gitelman syndrome. | Severe potassium depletion. | Current use of thiazides and loop diuretics. | Hypomagnesaemia | : the mechanism probably involves hypokalemia, which is usually caused by or associated with magnesium depletion. | ⚠ Important: | Key discriminator: | hypertension + chloride-resistant alkalosis | → think hyperaldosteronism / Cushing / Liddle; | normotension | → think Bartter / Gitelman / K | + | or Mg | 2+ | depletion.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Clinical Features | History | Helpful in establishing the | etiology | , e.g. GI fluid loss, surgery, drug history, or renal insufficiency. | Symptoms: | not specific | . | Hypoventilation | because of inhibition of the respiratory centers. | Symptoms of | hypokalemia | , e.g. weakness, myalgia, polyuria, and cardiac arrhythmias. | Symptoms of | hypocalcemia | (e.g. perioral tingling, muscle cramps and carpopedal spasms) due to decreased ionized calcium. | Signs | Also not specific but may help to establish the cause. | Volume depletion | usually accompanies chloride-responsive alkalosis, while | volume expansion | accompanies chloride-resistant alkalosis. | There may be signs of | hypocalcaemia | , e.g. | tetany, Chvostek sign, and Trousseau sign | . | Change in | mental status | , or | seizures | . | Key clinical clue | Volume status on examination points to the subtype: | volume depleted | → chloride-responsive; | volume expanded | → chloride-resistant.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Investigations | General investigations | → for the diagnosis of metabolic alkalosis. | ABG | (arterial blood gases): pH, HCO | 3 | − | , CO | 2 | Serum electrolytes | : Na | + | , K | + | , Cl | − | , Ca | 2+ | and Mg | 2+ | Urinary Cl | − | Specific investigations | → for determination of the etiology, e.g. | Plasma aldosterone and cortisol levels | Plasma renin activity | Reno-vascular imaging | NB: | Urine chloride (< 20 vs > 20 mEq/L) separates | chloride-responsive | from | chloride-resistant | alkalosis; hormone assays then target the specific etiology.

1B | Metabolic Alkalosis — Treatment | Treatment depends on the underlying etiology and on the patient’s volume status. | Treatment of chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis | Patients with volume depletion | Infusion of | isotonic (0.9% NaCl) sodium chloride | to correct alkalosis and restore volume. | Potassium chloride | (I.V. or oral) to correct the hypokalemia, if present. | Patients with volume overload (edematous states) | Potassium chloride | (I.V. or oral) to correct the alkalosis and avoid volume overload. | Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors | or | potassium-sparing diuretics | can be used to decrease volume and correct the alkalosis. | Treatment of chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis | Management is based on the | specific cause | (e.g. treat hyperaldosteronism, stop diuretics, replace Mg | 2+ | /K | + | ).

02 | Hyponatremia — Definition | Definition | A decrease in serum sodium concentration to a level | below 135 mmol/L | . | Dilutional hyponatremia | It is the | most common form | of the disorder and is caused by | water retention | rather than sodium depletion. | Pseudohyponatremia | A | spuriously low | plasma sodium concentration; the measured sodium concentration is low, but the | true physiological plasma sodium concentration is normal | . | Pseudohyponatremia can occur in any clinical situation in which the | serum lipids or protein concentration is markedly increased | to maintain plasma osmolality. | NB: | Always check the | plasma osmolality | : in true hypotonic hyponatremia it is low; in pseudohyponatremia it remains normal (iso-osmolar) — the sodium is diluted by excess lipid/protein in the measuring cup.

02 | Hyponatremia — Pathological Effects & Clinical Manifestations | Pathological effects | Hyponatremia leads to | shift of water from the ECF to the ICF | compartments. | Increased ICF volume leads to | cell swelling | . | In the brain this leads to | brain oedema | and neurologic manifestations. | Clinical manifestations | Manifestations of the | cause | . | Manifestations of hyponatremia ( | neurologic symptoms | ): changes in mental status including altered personality, lethargy, and confusion. | As the serum sodium falls: | stupor, neuromuscular hyperexcitability, hyperreflexia, seizures, coma, and death | can result. | ⚠ Important: | The severity of neurologic symptoms correlates well with the | severity | and the | rate of development | of hyponatremia.

02 | Hyponatremia — Classification & Clinical Types | Classification and clinical types | Hyponatremia states can be classified into | three types | according to plasma osmolality (tonicity): | Hypertonic, Isotonic and Hypotonic | . | The first two types, | Hypertonic and Isotonic | , can be considered as | pseudohyponatremia | while the last type, | Hypotonic | , is considered | true hyponatremia | . | Hypotonic Hyponatremia is classified into | three subtypes | according to the | volume status | of the patient. | Hyponatremia | Hypotonic | Hypervolemic | Euvolemic | Hypovolemic | Isotonic | Hypertonic | NB: | Isotonic & hypertonic = pseudohyponatremia; hypotonic (true) hyponatremia → classify by volume status.

02 | Hyponatremia — Causes | Hypervolemic Hyponatremia | Euvolemic Hyponatremia | Hypovolemic Hyponatremia | Heart failure | Liver failure | Oliguric AKI | CKD | Nephrotic syndrome | Hypoalbuminemia | SIADH | (Syndrome of Inappropriate Anti Diuretic Hormone secretion). | Nephrogenic syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis. | Primary polydipsia | Thiazide Diuretics. | Hypothyroidism. | Extra-renal loss | (vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, pancreatitis) | Renal loss | (diuretics, adrenal insufficiency, TIN, recovery phase of AKI) | How to read the table | Hypervolemic | : water excess with edema (edematous states). | Euvolemic | : no edema, SIADH is the prototype. | Hypovolemic | : sodium + water loss (extra-renal or renal).

02 | Hyponatremia — Diagnostic Algorithm | Diagnostic algorithm — types and causes of hyponatremia (flowchart) | Hyponatremia | → | Plasma osmolality | Low osmolality → EVS (extracellular volume status) | Increased | → consider | heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrosis | Normal | → urine osmolality: | < 100 mOsm/kg H | 2 | O → consider | polydipsia | > 100 mOsm/kg H | 2 | O → consider | SIADH, hypothyroidism, or hypocortisolism | Decreased | → consider | gastrointestinal fluid loss, Addison disease, salt-losing nephritis or cerebral salt wasting | Normal or high osmolality | Consider | hyperglycemia | or | pseudohyponatremia | NB: | EVS = extracellular volume status. The algorithm begins with | plasma osmolality | to separate true (hypotonic) from pseudo hyponatremia, then uses | volume status | and | urine osmolality | to reach the cause.

02 | Hyponatremia — Treatment | General principles | Primary goal is to | control symptoms | , then to | correct Na | + | level | . | Determine whether hyponatremia is | acute or chronic | . | Be careful of the | rate of correction | according to the rate of development (acute or chronic) to avoid | osmotic demyelination | , i.e. | central pontine myelinolysis | . | The fluid of choice for correction depends on the | volume status | of the patient. | Medications | Fluid / drug | Indicated states | Isotonic 0.9% NaCl | Hypo- and euvolemic states | Hypertonic 3% NaCl + Loop diuretics | Hyper- and euvolemic states | Vasopressin receptor antagonists | : Conivaptan, Tolvaptan | — | ⚠ Important: | Too rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia may cause | osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) | — correct slowly in chronic cases.

03 | Hypernatremia — Definition & Pathogenesis | Definition | An increase in the serum sodium concentration to a level | above 145 mmol/L | . Hypernatremia is a | rare condition | and nearly always indicates a | water deficit | that always reflects a state of | hypertonicity | because sodium is an osmotically effective ECF solute. | Pathogenesis | Water deficiency | Free water deficient states: | total body water deficit > total body sodium deficit | Excess solute | Excess water loss or | excess sodium retention | Lacks normal physiologic response | to free water loss: | ADH secretion | and | thirst | . | NB: | Normally, | ADH | (conserving water) and | thirst | (drinking water) defend against hypernatremia — hypernatremia therefore occurs when these defenses fail (e.g. unconscious, hypodipsia, diabetes insipidus).

03 | Hypernatremia — Pathological Effects & Clinical Manifestations | Pathological effects | Hypernatremia leads to | shift of water from the ICF to the ECF | compartments. | Reduction in the ICF volume and | cell shrinkage | . | In the brain this leads to | neurological sequelae | and | intracerebral hemorrhage | , often punctate, but sometimes major blood vessels disruption may occur. | Clinical manifestations | Manifestations of the | underlying condition | . | Manifestations of | ECF volume disturbances | . | Manifestations of | hypertonicity | : confusion, restlessness, hyperreflexia, spasticity, seizures and coma. | ⚠ Important: | Unlike hyponatremia (swelling), hypernatremia causes | cell shrinkage | — in the brain it can cause | intracerebral hemorrhage | .

03 | Hypernatremia — Classification & Clinical Types | Type | Mechanism | Examples | Hypervolemic Hypernatremia | Excessive IV sodium administration | Hypertonic (3%) saline | , | Sodium Bicarbonate | Euvolemic Hypernatremia | Renal water loss (low urine osmolality): | Diabetes Insipidus | Extra-renal water loss (high urine osmolality): | Rhabdomyolysis | — | Hypovolemic Hypernatremia | Renal sodium loss (high urine Na): | Diuretics, Polyuric ATN | Extra-renal sodium loss (low urine Na): | GIT, respiratory and skin loss | — | How to read the table | Hypervolemic | : sodium gain. | Euvolemic | : pure water loss (urine osmolality tells renal vs extra-renal). | Hypovolemic | : hypotonic fluid loss (urine Na tells renal vs extra-renal).

03 | Hypernatremia — Treatment | General principles | Primary goal is to | control volume loss (resuscitation) | , then | correct Na | + | level (maintenance) | . | During resuscitation, use fluid with volume of distribution confined to the | intravascular compartment | (i.e. isotonic), while use | hypotonic solutions | during maintenance. | 1. Rapid correction of severe ECF volume depletion (resuscitation) | Intravenous | Isotonic 0.9% NaCl | : volume and rate of infusion is guided by | clinical parameters | . | 2. Gradual replacement of fluid deficit (maintenance) | TBW deficit = 0.6 × premorbid weight (1 − [140/Na]) + daily requirements | Oral tap water in conscious patients or through an NG tube. If not feasible, use | Intravenous 5% Glucose | or | Half normal saline (0.45% NaCl) | . | ⚠ Important: | Correct | gradually | over hours to days | (0.5 to 1 mmol/L/hour) | to avoid | brain oedema | .

04 | Hyperkalemia — Definition & Causes (I. Increased Release) | Definition | An increase in S. potassium concentration to a level | above 5.5 mmol/L | . | I) Increased potassium release from the cells | Pseudo-hyperkalemia | : increased blood cell destruction | in vitro | (e.g. hemolysis) leading to K | + | release from the damaged cells — when blood samples are left for a long time at low temperature, especially in patients with | polycythemia or leukocytosis | . | Metabolic acidosis | Insulin deficiency | , hyperglycemia, and hyperosmolality | Increased tissue catabolism | : e.g. trauma, cytotoxic and radiation therapy for malignancy ( | tumor lysis syndrome | ). | β-adrenergic blockade | Exercise | Digitalis overdose.

04 | Hyperkalemia — Causes (II. Reduced Urinary Excretion) | II) Reduced urinary potassium excretion | Renal failure | ; due to decreased K | + | excretion. | Hypoaldosteronism | (primary and secondary). | Circulatory volume depletion | . | Type (IV) RTA | . | Drugs: | ACEIs, ARBs, NSAIDs, Cyclosporin | ; cause impaired angiotensin II induced aldosterone secretion → hypoaldosteronism → K | + | retention. | Potassium sparing diuretics (spironolactone) | , | trimethoprim antibiotic | , and | heparin | → aldosterone resistance → K | + | retention. | ⚠ Important: | Two drug mechanisms of K | + | retention: | impaired aldosterone secretion | (ACEIs / ARBs / NSAIDs / cyclosporin) vs | aldosterone resistance | (spironolactone / trimethoprim / heparin).

04 | Hyperkalemia — Manifestations | Manifestations | Elevation of the extracellular potassium concentrations results in a | decrease in cell membrane excitability | (especially nerve, muscle and cardiac cells) which is manifested by; | Muscle weakness or paralysis | , irritability, anxiety, paraesthesia, and/or | Impaired cardiac conduction | , irregular pulse and | cardiac standstill | (if hyperkalemia is sudden or severe). | Key concept — the membrane effect | High extracellular K | + | depolarizes | the resting membrane potential, making nerve/muscle/cardiac cells | less excitable | — hence weakness and cardiac conduction blocks.

04 | Hyperkalemia — Treatment (1. Membrane & 2. Cellular Shift) | ⚠ Important: | Urgent therapy is indicated when serious manifestations are present such as: | muscle weakness or paralysis, cardiac conduction abnormalities, cardiac arrhythmias, and/or serum K | + | concentration ≥ 7 mmol/L | . | 1. Stabilize the myocardial cell membrane | I.V. | calcium gluconate | , | 10 mg in 10 ml over 10 minutes | , as calcium antagonizes the cellular effects of hyperkalemia (a | physiologic antidote | ). | 2. Drive extracellular K | + | into the cells | (increase Na | + | /K | + | -ATPase pump activity) | Agent | Dose | Notes | β2 agonists | (albuterol, salbutamol) | 10 to 20 mg inhaled over 10 minutes | Peak effect in 90 minutes. Contraindicated in patients with ischemic heart diseases | Insulin and glucose | One ampule dextrose 50% concentration with 5–10 units of regular insulin I.V. | Peak effect within 60 min, lasts several hours. Side effect: | hypoglycemia | Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO | 3 | ) | — | Rapid effect within few minutes but | not long lasting

04 | Hyperkalemia — Treatment (3. Removal & 4. Monitoring) | 3. Removal of potassium from the body | Method | Mechanism / Notes | 1- Loop diuretics | Lead to K | + | loss in the urine by inhibiting Na/K/Cl transporter in loop of Henle. | 2- Potassium exchange resins | (sodium polystyrene sulfate) | Given orally or per rectum. Exchanges Na | + | for K | + | and binds it in the gut (primarily in large intestine) → decreasing total body K | + | . K | + | is removed in the stool, 8–12 hours after administration. | Side effects: intestinal necrosis / gangrene | . | 3- Hemodialysis | In | refractory and emergency cases | (i.e. high K | + | level > 7 mmol/L or ECG changes). | 4- Monitoring | Continuous | cardiac monitoring | and serial ECGs. | Measurement of | serum potassium at 1–2 hours | after the initiation of therapy.

04 | Hyperkalemia — ECG Changes | ECG changes of hyperkalemia | With rising serum K | + | , the ECG shows a | progressive sequence | : | Early | Tall peaked T waves | Intermediate | Prolonged PR intervals · ST segment depression · loss of P waves | Late / severe | Widened QRS · VT · cardiac standstill | Figure: ECG changes of severe hyperkalemia. | Tall peaked T waves → PR prolongation → P wave flattening/loss → QRS widening → sine wave → VT/VF → standstill. | ⚠ Important: | ECG changes are an | emergency trigger | — treat immediately even while awaiting the lab K | + | result.
