05 | Hypokalemia — Definition & Causes | Definition | A decrease in the S. potassium concentration to a level | below 3.5 mmol/L | . | Causes | Spurious hypokalemia; | occurs when a blood sample is kept in the blood tube for a long period at room temperature. This allows K | + | to enter the cells → falsely lower serum K | + | level. Particularly seen with | marked leukocytosis | and when | insulin is given just prior to blood drawing | . | Decreased K | + | intake | (normal daily K | + | intake = 40 – 120 mmol). | Shift of K | + | into the cells; | e.g. alkalosis, insulin therapy, β agonists and stress. | Renal K | + | loss; | e.g. | Diuretics | → activates renin angiotensin aldosterone system (RAAS) hyperaldosteronism → salt retention and potassium loss. | Hyperaldosteronism | / steroids therapy. | Proximal RTA | Hypomagnesaemia. | Polyuria. | Extra-renal K | + | loss; | e.g. loss of gastric fluid (persistent vomiting and gastric aspiration) leads to: | Loss of H | + | → increases plasma bicarbonate → | alkalosis | → ↑ cellular K | + | uptake. | Coexisting | volume depletion | → increases aldosterone secretion.

05 | Hypokalemia — NB: Associated Syndromes | NB: Syndromes associated with hypokalemia | Hypokalemic periodic paralysis | Results from a defect in a | voltage-gated calcium channel | . | Triggered by; | strenuous exercise followed by rest, high carbohydrates or sodium meals, and sudden changes in temperature | . | Bartter’s syndrome | The defect is impaired | Na Cl reabsorption in the loop of Henle | . | Salt loss → volume depletion and activation of the RAAS; findings are | similar to administration of a loop diuretic | . | Increased urinary calcium. | The syndrome is usually diagnosed in | childhood | , sometimes associated with growth and mental retardation. | Gitelman’s syndrome | The defect is in the | Na Cl transporter | . | Findings | mimic administration of a thiazide diuretic | . | NB: | Compare: | Bartter | = loop of Henle defect (like a loop diuretic, hypercalciuria); | Gitelman | = distal Na-Cl transporter defect (like a thiazide).

05 | Hypokalemia — Manifestations | Symptoms | GIT; | nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, constipation. | Muscles; | muscle weakness or cramps, paralysis. | CNS; | paraesthesia, psychosis, delirium, hallucinations, depression. | Renal; | polyuria, nocturia → polydipsia. | Cardiac; | palpitation. | Signs | GIT; | ileus. | CVS; | hypotension, bradycardia or tachycardia, premature beats, arrhythmias. | Respiratory; | hypoventilation, respiratory distress, respiratory failure. | CNS; | mental changes (e.g. lethargy), decreased muscle strength, fasciculation, tetany, decreased tendon reflexes. | ECG changes | ST- segments and T- waves depression | with | prominent U- waves | . | (Figure: ECG changes of hypokalemia.)

05 | Hypokalemia — Treatment | Treatment | Control the cause. | Potassium therapy: | I.V. Potassium chloride infusion | , when serum K | + | is | < 2.5 mmol/L | . The maximal rate of correction should be | less than 20 mmol/hour | . | Oral potassium | is the preferred route for K | + | depletion in other cases. | NB: | Cellular shift of K | + | into the cells requires | less potassium | to correct than hypokalemia from potassium loss. | Monitoring | Check | serum Mg levels | , since it is difficult to restore potassium if the former is low. | ECG monitoring | is required.

03 | Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease (ARPKD) | Hereditary Polycystic Kidney Disease | A rare autosomal recessive disorder with a defect on chromosome 6 — parents are not affected.

Cystic Kidney Diseases · ARPKD | Incidence & Symptoms | Incidence | A rare | autosomal recessive (AR) | disorder with a defect on | chromosome 6 | . | Parents are not affected | and occurrence in sibling is | variable | . | When Does It Present? | Presentation may be seen in the | perinatal period | , | early childhood | or | early adulthood | . | Perinatal presentation: | high mortality due to | pulmonary hypoplasia | . | High-Yield: | Perinatal presentation of ARPKD → | pulmonary hypoplasia | → high mortality.

Cystic Kidney Diseases · ARPKD | Treatment | Neonatal Presentation | No good treatment | . | Childhood | CKD | and | liver disease | are treated | as usual | . | Hypertension | and | UTIs | are treated | aggressively | .
04 | Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Chronic Kidney Disease complicating Arterial Hypertension | Clinical diagnosis in chronic hypertension — risk factors, criteria of diagnosis and management.

Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Definition | Definition | Generally, the term | hypertensive nephrosclerosis | is used for | chronic kidney disease | which | complicates arterial hypertension (AHT) | . | Key Point: | It is a diagnosis based on | clinical criteria | , not renal biopsy criteria.

Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Risk Factors | Demographic | Age (> 50 years) | Male gender | Low socioeconomic status | Family history | of hypertensive nephrosclerosis | Lifestyle | Cigarette smoking | Hypertension & Metabolic | Systolic hypertension | (persistently high) | Dyslipidemia | Proteinuria | Decreased GFR

Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Diagnosis — Clinical Criteria (Not Biopsy) | The diagnosis of hypertensive nephrosclerosis is generally based on | clinical criteria | not renal biopsy criteria. | The 5 Clinical Criteria of Diagnosis | History of | prolonged hypertension (> 10 years) | . | Low grade proteinuria (< 2 gm/day) | . | Grade I or II hypertensive retinopathy | . | Small scarred kidneys | . | No evidence of primary renal disease | .

Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Management — Diuretics | Diuretics — Cornerstone in CKD | Diuretics are commonly used | and represent the | cornerstone | in the management of CKD patients. | In general, as | GFR falls | , | higher doses of diuretics | are needed to achieve a | natriuretic response | . | Physiology Link: | Falling GFR → higher diuretic doses required → the dose is titrated to achieve a natriuretic response.

Hypertensive Nephrosclerosis | Antihypertensive Drugs (2/2) | 4- Mineralocorticoid (Aldosterone) Antagonists | Constitute an | important fourth-line BP agent | in the treatment of | resistant HTN | in later stages of CKD. | However, | risks of hyperkalemia and AKI | have | limited | mineralocorticoid antagonist use in | advanced CKD | . | 5- Other Agents | Other agents are used when | treatment with the other agents have failed | . | Important: | MRA use in advanced CKD is limited by the risks of | hyperkalemia | and | AKI | .
